learningObjectives.title: Beliefs about the causes of disease

questions.q: According to the medieval Theory of the Four Humours, the body contained blood, phlegm and which other two humours?
options: Yellow bile and black bile
Acid and alkali
Lymph and bile
Water and salt
questions.explain: The four humours were blood, phlegm, yellow bile and black bile, which physicians believed had to stay in balance.

questions.q: What did people who believed in miasma think caused disease?
options: Bad air or unpleasant smells from rotting matter
Tiny living germs in the blood
An excess of black bile
Contaminated drinking water
questions.explain: Miasma theory held that disease was caused by poisonous 'bad air' given off by decaying material and filth.

questions.q: During the Black Death of 1348-49, a person who believed the plague was a punishment from God would most likely respond by...
options: Praying, going on pilgrimage or joining the flagellants
Boiling their drinking water before use
Being vaccinated against the disease
Taking a course of antibiotics
questions.explain: Believing the plague was divine punishment, many turned to prayer, pilgrimage and self-flagellation to seek God's forgiveness.

questions.q: A medieval doctor bleeds a patient suffering from a fever to make them better. Which belief is his treatment based on?
options: The Theory of the Four Humours
Germ Theory
The idea that disease is spread by water
Vaccination
questions.explain: Bloodletting aimed to remove an excess of blood and restore the balance of the four humours.

questions.q: Which ancient Greek physician is credited with first developing the Theory of the Four Humours?
options: Hippocrates
Galen
Andreas Vesalius
Louis Pasteur
questions.explain: Hippocrates developed the Theory of the Four Humours, which later influenced Roman and medieval medicine.

questions.q: Why did the medieval Church encourage people to accept the ideas of the Roman physician Galen?
options: Galen believed the body was designed by a creator, which fitted Christian teaching
Galen had rejected all belief in God
Galen had proved that germs caused disease
Galen argued against the Theory of the Four Humours
questions.explain: Galen's belief that the body was made by a creator matched Christian ideas, so the Church promoted his work and discouraged challenges to it.

questions.q: Using Galen's Theory of Opposites, how might a physician treat a patient thought to have too much phlegm, a humour seen as cold and wet?
options: Give something hot and dry, such as pepper
Give something cold and wet, such as cucumber
Bleed the patient to remove blood
Isolate the patient to avoid bad air
questions.explain: The Theory of Opposites treated an imbalance with its opposite, so a cold, wet excess of phlegm was countered with hot, dry foods like pepper.

questions.q: Why did the work of Vesalius on anatomy and Harvey on the circulation of the blood have little immediate effect on the treatment of patients?
options: It improved understanding of the body but did not provide new cures
Their findings were quickly proved to be completely wrong
No doctors were able to read their published books
Their work led directly to the discovery of antibiotics
questions.explain: Their discoveries advanced knowledge of how the body worked but did not yet offer new treatments, so day-to-day care changed little.

questions.q: In 1796 Edward Jenner developed a vaccination against smallpox. Which mild disease did he use to give protection?
options: Cowpox
Measles
Cholera
Typhoid
questions.explain: Jenner used matter from cowpox sores to protect people against the far deadlier smallpox.

questions.q: Why did Jenner's smallpox vaccination face opposition when it was introduced?
options: He could not explain how or why it actually worked
It was proved to give people smallpox every time
It was far more expensive than earlier treatments
The Church officially banned all forms of medicine
questions.explain: Because germ theory was not yet known, Jenner could not explain why vaccination worked, which fuelled suspicion and opposition.

questions.q: Why was Louis Pasteur's Germ Theory, published in 1861, a turning point in beliefs about the causes of disease?
options: It showed that microbes in the air cause decay and disease
It confirmed that disease was caused by an imbalance of humours
It proved that all disease came from bad air alone
It showed that disease was solely a punishment from God
questions.explain: Pasteur's Germ Theory demonstrated that microbes caused decay and disease, overturning older ideas such as miasma and spontaneous generation.

questions.q: What was Robert Koch's key contribution to the understanding of disease?
options: He identified the specific microbes that cause particular diseases
He discovered the circulation of the blood
He introduced antiseptics into surgery
He founded the National Health Service
questions.explain: Koch built on germ theory by identifying the specific bacteria responsible for individual diseases, such as anthrax and tuberculosis.

questions.q: A town cleans up its water supply and the number of cholera cases falls sharply. Whose ideas does this best support?
options: John Snow
Galen
Hippocrates
Edward Jenner
questions.explain: John Snow argued cholera was spread through contaminated water, so cleaner water reducing cases supports his conclusions.

questions.q: Why was John Snow's 1854 investigation of the Broad Street cholera outbreak so significant?
options: It provided evidence that cholera was spread by water, not bad air
It proved that cholera was caused by an imbalance of humours
It discovered the antibiotic that cured cholera
It showed that cholera could only be caught from animals
questions.explain: By linking deaths to the Broad Street pump, Snow gave strong evidence that cholera spread through water rather than miasma, even before germ theory was accepted.

questions.q: Which substance did Joseph Lister introduce to fight infection during surgery?
options: Carbolic acid
Chloroform
Penicillin
Ether
questions.explain: Lister used carbolic acid as an antiseptic to kill germs during and after operations, greatly reducing infection.

questions.q: How did Pasteur's Germ Theory help Joseph Lister to develop antiseptic surgery?
options: It suggested that killing germs could prevent wounds becoming infected
It proved that surgery should be carried out without any washing
It showed that infection was caused by an imbalance of humours
It explained that anaesthetics were unnecessary during operations
questions.explain: Knowing that germs caused infection, Lister reasoned that destroying them with antiseptics like carbolic acid would keep wounds clean.

questions.q: In 1847 James Simpson discovered that chloroform could be used in medicine as a...
options: Anaesthetic to put patients to sleep during surgery
Antiseptic to clean wounds
Vaccine against smallpox
Antibiotic to kill bacteria
questions.explain: Simpson found that chloroform was an effective anaesthetic, allowing patients to be unconscious and pain-free during operations.

questions.q: Why did the number of deaths from surgery at first stay high even after anaesthetics were introduced?
options: Surgeons attempted longer, deeper operations, causing more bleeding and infection
Anaesthetics made patients immune to all disease
Antibiotics were being overused at the same time
Hospitals had stopped admitting any patients
questions.explain: Anaesthetics let surgeons operate more deeply, but before antiseptics this often led to more blood loss and infection, a period sometimes called the 'black period of surgery'.

questions.q: What did Alexander Fleming discover in 1928?
options: Penicillin, the first antibiotic
The circulation of the blood
The smallpox vaccine
The Theory of the Four Humours
questions.explain: Fleming discovered that the penicillin mould killed bacteria, marking the start of antibiotics, later mass-produced by Florey and Chain.

questions.q: Why was the creation of the National Health Service in 1948 a major change in approaches to treatment in Britain?
options: It provided healthcare that was free for everyone at the point of use
It made all medical treatment more expensive than before
It ended the use of hospitals across the country
It relied entirely on the Theory of the Four Humours
questions.explain: The NHS, set up in 1948, gave the whole population access to medical care free at the point of use, funded through taxation.
